text_narrative: The umpire's report on the second heat named the bow pair rather than the crew. Both blades entered late at the catch and came out square at the finish, and the boat checked twice in the middle of the course. Reddan, who coached the crew, timed the recovery from the launch and found a quarter second of gap. The crew rowed the heat out and lost by a length to a slower eight.
text_nonnarrative: A fault at the catch is classed apart from a fault at the finish, whatever the length of the stroke between them. A blade entering late puts the boat in one class of check; a blade leaving square puts it in a second, and the two are independent. Neither turns on the recovery. The crew, not the bow pair, is the unit graded over a course, and the heat is the unit reported.

text_narrative: Twenty-eight and holding, and the rate card in the boat says thirty-two for this stretch. Ilva calls twenty-eight anyway. The stroke's shoulders are going up and the puddles are shallowing, and a rating she cannot hold is worse than one she can. She calls the change at the buoy, gets thirty inside four strokes, and does not look at the card again for the rest of the piece.
text_nonnarrative: A call was faulted on the rating held and not on the rating named. A rate below the card figure counted as one departure; a rate the boat could not hold for the length of the piece counted as another, and the second was the graver. A change taken at a buoy was neither. It was the stroke count over the piece, not the voice, that fixed the class.

text_narrative: The rigging shed smelled of linseed, and the tape measure was the only thing in it that anyone trusted. Bern set the span at one metre sixty and marked the gate with a pencil ring. The pin height came out ten millimetres above the seat line on the stroke side and eight on the other. He shimmed the low side, remeasured, and left the boat on the trestles overnight.
text_nonnarrative: A rig was faulted on the span and on the pin height, and the two were classed apart. A span outside the stated band put the boat in one class whatever the gate; a difference of pin height between the two sides put it in another, and a shim under one seat did not remove the first. The trestles bore on nothing. Rigging, not the sculler, was the subject of the class.

text_narrative: Everyone in the harbour had an opinion about the handicap on the black cutter, and none of the opinions agreed. She rated at forty seconds a mile and finished ahead of the fleet in light air three seasons running. One summer the committee cut her allowance to twenty. She came second that year, and the same men who had complained about the forty complained about the twenty.
text_nonnarrative: A handicap is graded on the measured rating and never on the record of finishes. A boat finishing ahead of the fleet in light air is not thereby misrated; wins across a range of conditions bear on the rating, and a run of them in one condition bears on nothing. The allowance in seconds a mile follows from the measurement. What a committee corrects is arithmetic, not a reputation.

text_narrative: Four pitchers come to the green hob on the moor every seventh evening, and the clay holds every mark. The first lays a ringer and the clay keeps the ring. The second lays a leaner and the clay keeps that too. The third throws short and the clay shows nothing at all. The fourth throws nothing, stands at the mark counting the others, and takes the game on the count.
text_nonnarrative: A pitch is graded on where the quoit lies and not on how it travels. A ringer, meaning a quoit encircling the hob, counts above a leaner whatever the clay shows; a quoit short of the mark counts nothing and is not a class of near miss. Distance from the hob settles ties between two leaners. The count at the close of a game, not the best pitch in it, fixes the result.

text_narrative: In the fifth season after the green at Ardleigh was relaid, the club found the pace running three seconds faster than the old turf and half the members' bowls unusable. The heaviest biased woods drew a full yard wide of the jack. A committee sat in the pavilion through August and ruled that the old woods might be used on the lower rink only. Eleven members left for the town club.
text_nonnarrative: Four biases make up an ordinary set of woods, of which the second is the most used on a fast green. Each wood is turned with one side heavier than the other, and the bias is stated as a number rather than a distance. The set also carries a jack, unbiased and lighter, and a mat. Nothing in a set is matched by weight alone; the pairing is by bias.

text_narrative: When the ice first covered the inland sea, the makers of the north went down and cut sixteen stones out of one grey outcrop, and dressed the running band of each by hand. Eight were dressed keen and eight were dressed dull. The keen eight ran further and curled less; the dull eight curled far and stopped short. The makers set them all in one house and never sorted them again.
text_nonnarrative: Sixteen stones made up a house set, of which the four hack stones were the heaviest. Each stone was dressed on a running band at the underside, and the band, not the whole face, was the bearing surface. Two handles came with each, of different colours, bolted through the crown. No two stones in the set were of exactly one weight, and the sorting was by band width alone.

text_narrative: There was a bear in a travelling company who could stand on one paw and hold the pose while a boy counted forty. The other beasts learned the easy holds and left the hard ones alone. One spring the bear tried a hold with both paws off the mat and came down on the matting, unhurt and much annoyed. After that she went back to the count of forty and no further.
text_nonnarrative: The standard sequence has six holds in all, of which the middle two are held the longest. Each is named for the part in contact with the mat: one hand, two hands, forearm, head, or shoulder. Two are held with the hips above the shoulders and four are not. The matting under the sequence is a separate item of the kit, thicker at the centre than at the edges.

text_narrative: The notebook on the dead man's desk is open at a page of opening lines and one of them is wrong. Inspector Varhelm cannot play, but she can see that the fourth move in the second column is in a different ink. Three other pages carry the same ink at the same depth in the line. She takes the notebook away, and the sergeant marks the desk with tape.
text_nonnarrative: What was admired in a broad repertoire was mostly the labour behind it, which was the least useful thing about it. The value of a set of opening lines lay in how far it carried a player who had not memorised the branches, and a wide repertoire was thin everywhere. Defences on the ground of surprise were not empty, but surprise was a property of the opponent rather than of the lines.

text_narrative: Three times that winter the old canon set the same ending on the board for the novices, and three times nobody found the drawing move. In November a boy pushed the pawn and lost. In December another boy moved the king the wrong way along the rank and lost. In January the smallest of them left the pawn where it stood and moved the rook one square.
text_nonnarrative: Endings are praised for their purity and the praise is usually misplaced, since purity is a matter of how few pieces remain. A composed ending has its standing from the narrowness of the drawing line and not from the count of material on the board. Objections from the side of practical play have some force; positions of that kind rarely arise. They arise often enough to matter.

text_narrative: Nobody in the back room of the inn would play the man with the grey gloves twice, and it had to do with the way he forced. He never took unless taking was compelled, and then he took the whole board in one long chain, eleven pieces, every time. The chain was always eleven. A carter counted it on four separate evenings and got eleven on all four.
text_nonnarrative: The compulsion to capture was defended as the thing that gave the game its depth, and that was the wrong reason to admire it. What the rule did was narrow the branching, so that a line could be seen a long way with little effort. The complaint that it removed judgement had something in it, but it removed judgement from the taking and put it into the offering.

text_narrative: Nine stones on the board before the first move, and the elder of the tower still calls it a game between equals. Which it is not. Vessa sets the ninth stone on the far corner point and considers what the word equal is doing in the sentence. Her opponent has waited three hundred years for a game and will not be hurried. She passes the bowl across and waits.
text_nonnarrative: A handicapped game and an even game were either one game or two under a single name, and counting stones did not settle which. If the placement was part of the position, then no rule had been altered and the two were one game. If the placement was a concession made before play, the second game had a rule the first lacked, and the identity failed.

text_narrative: In the long crossing, when the fleets still sang to keep the watches together, the first conductor of the outer ships beat time with both hands and no sound at all. Her pattern was of six, though every voice she led counted in four. For nine hundred watches the two counts held together and nobody could say why. The pattern of six was still beaten on the older ships long after.
text_nonnarrative: The ambiguity whether a beat pattern was a description of the music or an instrument of it was a real difficulty in the art and not a mere quibble. On one account the pattern reported a division present in the bar, and a singer able to read had no need of it. On another the division was owed to the hand, in which case the pattern was constitutive rather than merely reportive.

text_narrative: A gaming room above a chandler's shop loses its licence over a leather shaker with a lip inside it. The room's own man, Delkes, states that the lip is wear and nothing else. Two hundred throws made in front of the licensing clerk give six twice as often as chance allows. The shaker goes into an envelope, the licence goes onto the fire, and the room reopens as a coffee house.
text_nonnarrative: Fairness in a die was a claim about the object or about the throwing, and the two were not the same claim. Taken as a claim about the object, fairness was a matter of symmetry in the mass, and no run of throws established it. Taken as a claim about a practice, fairness belonged to the shaker and the hand together, and the object alone had no such property.

text_narrative: There was an alley behind a chapel where the pins set themselves. A wheelwright played there alone on winter nights and found that the nine came up in a different frame every time, never the diamond and never the square. One night the pins stood in a single row facing him down the alley. He rolled the cheese straight down the boards and took all nine, and the alley was empty after that.
text_nonnarrative: The chance of a full house falls roughly as the square of the number of pins standing off the true spot. The constant belongs to the alley and to the width of the cheese rather than to the player at the mark. For one or two pins off spot the relation is close enough to linear; past four it does not hold, and the frame itself is then the governing quantity.

text_narrative: The wire over the square is tuned like a string, and the man who tunes it will not say to what. Arnau walks out to the middle and the note under his feet is a fourth below the one he set at dawn. Nobody has touched the winch. He stands at the centre, waits for the note to come back up, and it does, and he walks on to the far pole.
text_nonnarrative: Sag at the middle was inversely proportional to the tension in the line and directly proportional to the weight carried. The constant was a property of the wire itself and of the distance between the two poles. For small loads the relation was near enough exact; beyond a load of a tenth of the breaking figure it did not hold, and the wire's own weight was no longer a negligible term.

text_narrative: Four run-throughs in one afternoon, and the sixth club is the one that decides them. On the first the clubs come round a half turn fast and the pattern climbs. On the second Petra throws lower and the turns come right. On the third she adds the sixth club and the turns go slack again. On the fourth she throws the sixth higher than the rest and the pattern holds.
text_nonnarrative: Time in the air is proportional to the square root of the height thrown, and the number of turns follows from that time and the rate of spin given at release. The constant of spin is a property of the club, chiefly of where its mass lies along the handle. Below a certain height the relation is of no use, since the hand is in contact for much of the flight.

text_narrative: In the third year of the northern circuit, the company at Halveth hung a second bar four feet behind the first and altered the catch for a whole season. The flyer left the platform on the fifth swing instead of the third. Eleven catches in twelve came clean in rehearsal and seven in twelve came clean before an audience. The second bar came down in the autumn and was not hung again.
text_nonnarrative: Two bars hang in a rig, a fly bar and a catch bar, each on a pair of ropes from a separate beam. The fly bar carries a wooden core and a taped grip at the centre third; the catch bar has no grip and is the longer of the two. A safety net is a distinct part of the rig, laced to a frame that stands clear of both beams.

text_narrative: Five strings where there ought to be four, and the fifth goes up into the dark above the bridge and is fastened to nothing. Yorwen counts them again. The head string, the two shoulder strings, the back string, and the fifth. The puppet lifts its left hand when nobody is at the bar. She winds all five onto the perch, hangs it in the case, and locks the case.
text_nonnarrative: A figure was strung from the head, the shoulders and the back, with a string to each hand and, in the larger sorts, one to each knee. The head string bore most of the weight and was the shortest. Shoulder strings stood in a pair, of equal length, and were the only strings crossed above the bridge. A string to the spine was absent from the simpler figures.

text_narrative: Nobody in the family would let the youngest hold the control bar, and the reason was an old one about her grandmother's hands. The bar had a rocker for the legs and a slide for the head, and the slide had worn to a shape that fitted one grip and no other. The youngest's hands were her grandmother's hands exactly. When she took the bar at fourteen, the slide fitted her.
text_nonnarrative: A control comprised a main bar, a rocker hinged across it, and a slide let into the upper face. The main bar took the head and back strings; the rocker took the two leg strings and turned about a pin at its centre. The slide carried the head string alone and lay fore and aft along the main bar. A second rocker for the hands was absent from the older controls.

text_narrative: A touring company cancels three nights in a row over a fault nobody can find in the screen. The cloth is new, the lamp is new, and the frame has been rebuilt twice. On each of the three nights a fourth figure appears on the cloth between the third and fourth scenes, in silhouette, held by no rod. The company packs the screen into its case and travels on without it.
text_nonnarrative: The cloth was stretched on a frame and carried on two uprights, with the lamp behind it on a boom at the height of the figures. Sharpness of edge was a function of the distance from figure to cloth and of the size of the source, and was independent of the brightness. Without a mask at the frame the lit field was wider than the cloth on all four sides.

text_narrative: In the age of the deep houses, the joiners of the third city cut a trap in the boards of every stage and swore an oath about what the traps were for. Each trap had a counterweight of lead and a bridle of hemp. On the night the last of the joiners went down through one, the bridle held and the weight did not come up, and the trap stayed open until morning.
text_nonnarrative: A trap was a hinged or sliding leaf in the stage floor, carried on a cradle below and balanced by a counterweight on a line over a head sheave. The travel of the cradle was set by the length of the line and by the depth of the cellar, and the two were fixed independently. Without a bridle at the leaf, the cradle and the leaf were not constrained together.

text_narrative: Twice in one run the flying cue at the civic hall went wrong by the same eleven pounds. On the first occasion the operator had loaded for the understudy and the principal went up. On the second the ballast bag had been left in the wings. Between the two the house carpenter chalked the weight of every performer on the inside of the loft rail, and the cue held.
text_nonnarrative: A single flight is set apart from a compound flight by the number of lines under load rather than by the distance travelled. Assisted flight is a third sort, marked off from both in that the counterweight carries less than the whole load and a hand takes the rest. A cue involving no vertical travel belongs to none of the three and is a track move.

text_narrative: A scene painter in the cliff theatre had flats that would not fall. She braced them with nothing at all, and the stagehands set them upright on the boards and let go, and they stood through a wind off the sea. A visiting master unscrewed one of her stiles to see the trick and found the timber hollow and full of sand. The flat stood anyway, and so did the stile.
text_nonnarrative: A braced flat is distinguished from a jacked flat by where the support meets the floor and not by the weight it carries. A booked pair is a third arrangement, set apart from both in that each leaf braces the other and the floor takes no fixing. A flat hung from above belongs to none of these three, since the matter of floor support does not arise for it.

text_narrative: In the second season after the pit at the civic rooms was lowered, the desks at the back lost sight of the beat and the players at the front lost sight of the stage. The librarian measured from every chair to the rostrum and found nine of thirty-four blind. A rail was cut down by eight inches over the winter, and six of the nine were recovered.
text_nonnarrative: The pit lay below the stage lip, its floor stepped in two shallow tiers with the rostrum on the upper one. Sight of the beat was clear from the front tier and broken from the two back corners, where the stage lip stood between. The rail along the house side was at the height of a seated player's eye. Behind the rostrum the floor was level for three desks.

text_narrative: Wind comes down the col in gusts and the line goes hard and soft in Marrit's hands like something breathing. The kite is a flat six-footer with a bridle she made from boot lace. She lets out forty yards and the pull settles at what feels like eight pounds. The gauge in her other hand says eleven. She takes in ten yards, gets nine on the gauge, and leaves it there.
text_nonnarrative: The col stood between two rounded summits, open to the west and closed on the eastern side by a low ridge of scree. The ground at the saddle was flat for some sixty yards and steep beyond it on both hands. The western approach lay in the lee of nothing at all. A stone shelter stood at the northern edge of the flat ground, below the level of the wind.

text_narrative: Everyone at the hall knew which rows to avoid, and the reason had nothing to do with the price. The rake was one in twelve at the front and one in eight at the back, and the change came at row K. People sitting in K and L saw the stage over the heads in front and people in J did not. The manager sold J at the same price for eleven years.
text_nonnarrative: Complaints about obstructed view vary more between rows of one house than between houses of one size. The median rake reported in returns of this kind is close to one in ten. Position of the change in gradient accounts for most of the spread within a house; the total number of rows accounts for very little. Managers describing their raked seating as uniform are a small minority of those returning figures.

text_narrative: The transit theatre on the ring reported eleven hundred admissions for a house of nine hundred and forty seats. Every stub matched a printed number and every number appeared once. The house manager pulled the whole roll and found that the counterfoil book had been printed twice from one plate, in two inks, and that the second printing had gone out unnumbered on the third night.
text_nonnarrative: Discrepancies between stubs held and seats sold were commoner in houses printing their own rolls than in those taking them from a central press. Within either group the scatter was wide, and the two distributions overlapped heavily. Doors in use accounted for more of the variation than size of house did. Something near a sixth of the houses returning figures reported no discrepancy of any kind.

text_narrative: Six bells left of the eight, and a method that wanted eight. Harran stood in the ringing chamber and worked out what could be rung on six by a band of four, two of them handling two ropes each. It could be done for a hundred and twenty changes and no further. Nobody in the valley had heard a peal in eleven years and would not know the difference.
text_nonnarrative: A method is a rule for permuting an order of bells, one place of change at a stroke, such that no order recurs before the whole is complete. Its length is fixed by the number of bells and by the places allowed at each change. A peal is therefore a defined quantity rather than a duration, and depends on the method named and not on the band.

text_narrative: In the year the wakes were moved to a later week, the six men of the lower village danced a figure with sticks that no other village would admit to knowing. It had eight bars where the neighbouring figures had six, and the clash came on the fourth and the eighth. A curate wrote the figure down in the parish book and drew the positions as small circles.
text_nonnarrative: A stick figure is a set dance in which each dancer holds one or two short staves and the pattern is marked by a clash between staves rather than by a step. Its length is counted in bars of the tune, and the clash falls at fixed bars within the set. The number of dancers is therefore not free, and is settled by the figure rather than by the company.

text_narrative: Before the seasons were fixed, the first people set a pole in the middle of the world and hung eighty ribbons from its crown, and the plaiting of those ribbons was what held the year together. Half the dancers went one way and half the other. In the year the count came out odd, one ribbon was left hanging and the summer ran short by a day.
text_nonnarrative: The pole is required to stand plumb and to carry an even number of ribbons, each of the full length from crown to ground. Ribbons are permitted in two colours only, alternating at the crown. Where a dancer is wanting, the ribbon is to be held by a bystander rather than left loose. No plait is allowable in which the two directions are unequal.

text_narrative: Heat comes off the lantern through the glove, and the gel in the frame is going brown at the middle. Iska pulls the frame, holds the new sheet against the light to check it, and slides it home. The focus is soft where the plot calls for hard. She reaches past the gate for the knurled ring, turns it half a turn, and the edge on the boards comes up clean.
text_nonnarrative: A gel is required to sit in a frame of the size stated for the lantern and never against the glass. Two sheets are permitted in one frame only where the plot names a double. Where a sheet is browned through more than a quarter of its area, it is to be drawn and replaced. No lantern is to be focused with the frame out of the runners.

text_narrative: No newcomer could play on the board in the taproom of the old house. The bed was chalked and rechalked until the lines stood proud of the slate, and a coin that stopped on a line counted for nothing. Regulars knew the four beds where the chalk was thin. A carter from twenty miles off won nine games in a row on his first evening, and was never seen again.
text_nonnarrative: Chalking a bed is treated as maintenance and it is nearer to composition, since the width of a line decides how much of the bed counts as a bed at all. A thick line narrows the target and favours a short stroke; a thin one does the reverse. It is true that players adapt within a few games, which is why the practice looks trivial, and why it is not.

text_narrative: Two systems of marking in one book, and both of them her mother's. Delyth turns to the third act and finds the warnings in pencil on the left and the standbys in red on the right, and then, from the middle of the act, the other way about. Something happened in that run. She copies the pencil marks over in red and leaves the change unexplained.
text_nonnarrative: A prompt book is described as a record and it is nearer to an instrument, since the marks in it are made to be acted on rather than consulted. The proof is that a book marked for one house is nearly useless in another. It is true that old books are read as history, and read well, but that is a use they acquire rather than their own.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the electric houses, the theatre at Brantwick fitted cue boxes at nine stations and abolished the whistle. Each box had a red lamp for standby and a white lamp for go. In the first month the white lamp at the fly floor failed twice, and both times the flyman took the loss of the red as his go and moved early.
text_nonnarrative: Standby: the state of a station warned but not released, shown by the red lamp alone. Go: the state shown by the white lamp, on which the station acted. Dark box: a station showing neither lamp, which was not a go and was to be queried. Station: any position fitted with a box and named on the plot. Double: two boxes wired to one switch at the desk.

text_narrative: Nobody in the saloon plays the corner table for money, and the reason is the third cushion. The rubber there has gone hard and takes an inch off the angle every time, and a man who learned the table can bank a ball three rails and put it where he wants. Newcomers see a shot that ought to sit and watch it come up short by a hand's width.
text_nonnarrative: Cushion: the rubber-faced rail against which a ball rebounded. Angle of return: the angle made with the cushion by a ball leaving it, measured from the same point as the angle of arrival. Short cushion: any rail returning a ball at less than the arriving angle. Bank: a stroke played to reach an object ball by way of one or more cushions. Rail count: the number of cushions so used.

text_narrative: The stewards at the county meeting disqualified the second team of the afternoon for an exchange made a foot beyond the zone. The outgoing runner had started level with the far line and the baton left the incoming hand outside the paint. Neither runner disputed it. A steward remeasured the zone with a tape and found the far line itself painted eight inches long.
text_nonnarrative: Exchange zone means the length of lane between the two painted lines, measured on the inner edge of the lane and inclusive of the paint. Where the baton passes from one hand to the other outside those limits, the exchange is void whatever the position of the runners. Nothing here bears on the placing of the runners. A zone wrongly marked is not a zone.

text_narrative: Three drivers take the same cone course in one morning and each of them loses a ball at a different pair. The first knocks the eleventh. The second knocks the eleventh and the third. The third driver stops the pair short of the eleventh, gets down, and finds the two cones set an inch closer than the wheels of any carriage in the county.
text_nonnarrative: Cone pair meant two markers set at a stated width apart, each carrying a ball at the crown. Displacement of a ball was a fault against the pair, and not against the driver or the horses. Where the width between markers was less than that stated for the class, the pair was void and no fault lay at it. Nothing in this affected the time recorded.

text_narrative: In the long dark between the two settlements, the crews played a game of thirteen tricks and made a law of it, and the law outlasted the crews. Whoever led the first trick led all the rest until a trick was lost. The oldest hand on the ship held the thirteenth card face up for everyone to see. Two ships that met in the dark would play a hand before they spoke.
text_nonnarrative: A card was playable only if it followed the suit led, or if the hand held none of that suit; a card played out of turn was not a play and stood withdrawn. Two cards laid together left the trick undecided and the lead unchanged. A gathered trick could not be looked at and could not be answered. Where no card was playable, the hand was void and the deal fell again.

text_narrative: There was a hedgehog on the lawn of a great house who understood the hoops better than the players. She would sit in the jaws of the second hoop and let a ball through only if the ball had run the first. A guest tried to lift her out and she rolled to the third hoop and sat there instead. That season no ball ran a hoop out of order on that lawn.
text_nonnarrative: A ball is through a hoop only if no part of it stands within the jaws with the stroke complete; a ball resting between the uprights is not through, and the point does not stand. Two balls in one hoop leave the order of play unchanged. A ball played out of turn is not a stroke and cannot be answered. Where a hoop is out of order, the point is not available.
